tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST
tiles.details: Texas wintergrass is a cool-season perennial tuft, often green while warm-season bluestems are dormant. Follow an attached spring panicle to ONE mature single-flowered spikelet. One long twisted and often twice-bent awn plus an elongated sharp callus support the ID; winter color alone cannot certify the species. Existing winter-tuft and flowering panels show useful gross traits, not a connected rooted specimen.
tiles.short: Winter-green bunch; in spring, follow ONE awned floret to a pointed seed base
tiles.status: FIELD-READY GROSS CUE; NEEDS SAME-PLANT ROOTED SPRING MATERIAL

tiles.heading: 02 · OPEN THE COLLAR
tiles.details: Open a fresh blade–sheath junction and inspect the very short glabrous truncate membranous ligule. Flora of North America reports ~0.2–1.2 mm (Kew ~0.4–0.7 mm), while adjacent collar hair tufts may reach ~0.5–1 mm. Photograph membrane and hairs separately at 10–20× with 0.5-mm scale. The archived sheath photo does not prove an accurately measured membrane.
tiles.short: True membrane ~0.2–1.2 mm; side hairs are NOT the ligule

tiles.heading: 03 · CHECK THE ONE-FLOWERED SPIKELET
tiles.details: In a fresh spring spikelet identify the paired pale 3–5-veined glumes enclosing ONE fertile floret. Flora of North America describes glumes ~10–21 mm; Kew gives lower ~10–17 mm and upper ~10–16 mm. When the ripe floret sheds, empty glumes can remain attached (panel 12). Measure the attached glumes and do not mistake an empty pair for a detached seed-bearing lemma.
tiles.short: Two persistent pale glumes ~10–21 mm (FNA); not the hardened seed-bearing lemma
tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — MEASURED GLUMES ON ONE ATTACHED SPIKELET

tiles.heading: 04 · FOLLOW THE HARD LEMMA TO ITS CALLUS
tiles.details: A mature fruit has a hardened rolled fertile lemma, a sharp often hairy basal callus and a pale apical crown. Kew reports a ~5.3–5.7 mm lemma body; FNA's ~6.5–13 mm floret figure is a DIFFERENT measurement, not a contradiction to erase. Callus ranges ~1–5.5 mm (FNA) and crown ~0.75–2 mm (FNA). Panels show actual hard fruit, but same-voucher calibrated callus and crown views remain needed.
tiles.short: Hard lemma ~5.3–5.7 mm (Kew); basal sharp hairy callus ~1–5.5 mm (FNA)

tiles.heading: 05 · COUNT THE AWNS ON ONE LEMMA
tiles.details: Trace the long awn from the actual hardened lemma tip: FNA gives ~40–90 mm and Kew ~50–60 mm. Do not count neighboring awns from different spikelets as branches of one awn. The sharp basal callus and apical pale crown should be photographed at the same time as the awn insertion; existing scaled Bob Harms photos show important gross parts but do not close every same-specimen microscopic hold.
tiles.short: ONE twisted, usually twice-bent awn ~40–90 mm (FNA); not three
tiles.status: FIELD-READY SINGLE-AWN CLUE; ATTACHMENT/CROWN SCALE GAP

tiles.heading: 06 · SEPARATE THREEAWNS AND FEATHERGRASS
tiles.details: Purple/oldfield threeawn (Aristida purpurea / A. oligantha) has three awn limbs arising from ONE lemma, unlike Texas wintergrass. Mexican feathergrass (Nassella tenuissima) ALSO has one long awn, but much finer tightly rolled leaves, smaller mature lemma and a short ~0.2–0.4 mm relatively blunt callus. Compare ripe fruits at the SAME scale. Little bluestem has multiple short silky racemes; wildryes form terminal spikes rather than this loose panicle.
tiles.short: Aristida has THREE awn limbs per lemma; Mexican feathergrass also has ONE but a tiny blunt callus
tiles.status: FIELD-READY LOOK-ALIKES; MATCHED FRUIT MICROPHOTOS MISSING

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: COOL-SEASON winter-green clump first: Texas wintergrass often greens during winter while warm-season grasses brown. At bloom in spring, the panicle is loose or somewhat narrowed with distinct long-awned individual spikelets, as the new Sam Kieschnick photo shows. Crucially, FOLLOW ONE mature floret to its ONE long, twisted and twice-bent awn attached to a hard lemma, then verify a long sharp hairy callus at the opposite base. The USDA example arrows show the callus, lemma and awn of ONE fruit. Nearby Aristida has THREE awn limbs from one lemma; cultivated Mexican feathergrass also has a single awn but a tiny blunt callus and thinner rolled foliage. New same-taxon actual Harms scaled photos show collar/sheath, spikelet flowers, mature one-awed hard fruit and empty glumes. The true ligule is a SHORT glabrous membranous structure often 0-1 mm and may appear absent. Do not mistake long collar hairs for the ligule or pale empty glumes for the hardened sharp fruit.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: Cool-season perennial tufted bunchgrass, often conspicuously green in winter in open native Central Texas grassland; can be up to 1.2 m tall in fruiting shoots.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Open a fresh blade–sheath junction and inspect the very short glabrous truncate membranous ligule. Flora of North America reports ~0.2–1.2 mm (Kew ~0.4–0.7 mm), while adjacent collar hair tufts may reach ~0.5–1 mm. Photograph membrane and hairs separately at 10–20× with 0.5-mm scale. The archived sheath photo does not prove an accurately measured membrane.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Open to sometimes rather contracted slender panicle, generally bearing well-spaced one-flowered spikelets rather than Aristida's trifid awn per lemma; FNA describes terminal panicles 5–55 cm with 1–4 spikelets on branchlets.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Aristida (oldfield and purple threeawn): THREE terminal lemma awn branches from ONE floret, rather than Nassella leucotricha's SINGLE awn. Mexican feathergrass N. tenuissima: ALSO has ONE long awn, but tightly hairlike rolled leaves, much SMALLER fertile lemma (~1.8–3.6 mm versus N. leucotricha ~5.3–13 mm across major descriptions), and a very short blunt callus (~0.2–0.4 mm vs leucotricha usually >1 mm). Little bluestem: warm-season with many short silky separate racemes along upper leafy branches, not a loose wintergreen needlegrass panicle. Canada and Virginia wildrye: cool-season grasses too, but bear multiple awned spikelets clustered into more obvious spikes; inspect floret awn placement and entire inflorescence.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: 1 · WINTER TUFT — actual green bunch among dry leaves
panels.image_role: Actual archived source-determined Texas wintergrass vegetative tuft; narrow live green blades in dry litter, no seedhead in this photograph
panels.caption: True pixel-inspected archived photograph shows multiple fine green blades arising in a dense small bunch amid brown fallen leaves and dry blades. This is HABIT evidence only: there is no exposed root/collar, no confirmed attached panicle, and no flowering character that independently determines the species.
panels.why_it_matters: Crew first look in late fall to spring: locate the green cool-season bunch, but wait for mature fruit before naming Texas wintergrass.
panels.creator: John Thomlinson
panels.photo_status: 2026-10-21 inspected actual 1400x933 JPEG stored in canonical folder, archived GBIF CC BY/John Thomlinson record; original exact photo license version and taxon independently unreviewed, retained provisional. One arrow marks visibly dense green leaf tuft only.
panels.photo_license_note: Individual archived photo recorded as CC BY; precise version not documented. Original source photo remains linked. Species determination can be provisional.
panels.modifications: Resaved JPEG with metadata removed (original source rights remain attached)

panels.label: 2 · SPRING HEAD — source-identified awned panicle in hand
panels.image_role: Real photographed Texas wintergrass open-to-narrow panicle with several attached slender sharp-looking spikelets and long awns against a hand
panels.caption: Archived Sam Kieschnick photograph visibly shows slender branching panicle with multiple narrow florets and exceptionally long threadlike AWNS, fingers behind for broad size. Photograph is not a dissection and cannot establish actual callus length, lemma corona or glume veins. Do NOT label multiple awn threads in this image as one three-awned Aristida fruit.
panels.why_it_matters: Links field recognition of a real awned spring flowering head to the USDA enlarged example showing ONE awn on ONE hardened lemma.
panels.creator: Sam Kieschnick
panels.photo_status: 2026-10-21 inspected actual 1050x1400 JPEG stored in canonical folder, archived GBIF CC BY/Sam Kieschnick record; source species determination follows recorded observation and original per-photo license version recheck desirable. Two conservative gross structure arrows, no invisible microscopic claims.
panels.photo_license_note: Individual archived photo recorded as CC BY; precise version not documented. Original source photo remains linked. Species determination can be provisional.

panels.label: Purple threeawn — three bristles arise from each lemma
panels.caption: PURPLE THREEAWN COMPARISON: typically three spreading branches arise from ONE lemma; Texas wintergrass has only ONE long awn on a floret. Count on the same mature lemma—not from a whole panicle.
panels.creator: Matt Lavin

memory_rule: Start with cool-season green bunch, THEN open spring panicle; trace ONE attached mature floret. One long twice-bent twisted AWN and an elongated sharp hairy CALLUS support Texas wintergrass. THREE limbs from one lemma = Aristida. One awn alone does not exclude Mexican feathergrass.
safety_note: New John Thomlinson and Sam Kieschnick archive JPEGs are recorded CC BY and physically installed already; genus/species source view now reuses them with full source credit. Neither shows an individual measured lemma/corona/collar. Archived CC BY version needs eventual photo-level license recheck. USDA detached fruit image is public domain but non-Hays; Abilene CC BY-NC is restricted to credited noncommercial deployment. Keep individual rights and county nativity determinations unchanged. Harms photos are copyrighted but explicitly reusable for scientific/educational displays with credit; NOT CC or broadly redistributable. Never infer original Hays collection from his broad Central Texas photo collection. Six exact Harms originals physically stored under limited educational permission, not CC; USDA PD image remains external, not counted as locally archived.
field_rule: Visible gross photos: winter-active bunch -> attached often loose spring flowering head. ID requires one mature floret with ONE long bent/twisted awn and an elongated sharp callus; one-awed Mexican feathergrass remains a lookalike. Threeawns have THREE limbs on ONE lemma, not three nearby separated florets.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
